items_missed: No agenda statement. 'Is this a good time to talk about your move?' is a permission ask, not a roadmap — the customer never heard what was coming, in what order, or how long it would take. That matters here because it cost her at the end: the customer's timer went off mid-close ('I'm sorry one sec. Sorry my timer for now'), which is what happens when nobody sets the expected length up front.
Never asked 'how are you today?' She opened 'Hi, good morning this is juline with Einstein moving' and went straight into the request confirmation — a greeting is not the check-in.

Packing services never asked about or offered. She asked the box question, got 'mostly it's just gonna be for like the bigger furniture,' logged 'furniture only, no boxes,' and moved on. A two-bedroom apartment moving with zero boxes means the customer is packing everything himself, or hasn't thought about it yet — either way 'we can also pack for you at the same hourly rate, and we bring all the materials' is revenue she never put on the table, and this customer booked, so it was live money.
Additional stops never asked.

Moving-stressor question never asked. She surfaced the TV concern only because the customer volunteered it; the open 'what are you most worried about with this move?' never came, and on a call where the customer had one specific anxiety, asking directly would likely have found more.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — she went straight to the number: 'here on Einstein. We charge an hourly rate which is $206 per hour for two movers.'

The rate was given as a team number, not per mover per hour. '$206 per hour for two movers already' hides the $103-per-mover structure, which is the figure customers use to compare against competitors quoting per person.

Day-of-week tiers never offered. This is a Saturday move quoted at the weekend rate of $206/hr, and the cheaper Sunday-through-Thursday tier was never mentioned — not as an option, not as a comparison, not even as context for why Saturday costs what it costs. Every other rep who had a weekend mover this week surfaced the cheaper days.
Packing service pricing never given, as a consequence of never asking about packing.

No Worries Damage Coverage delivered without its name or its full definition. 'We do have an additional insurance coverage that can cover you up to $2,000 per move. If there are any accidental damages' gets the number and the trigger right, but 'No Worries Damage Coverage' never lands as a brand, 'repair, replace, or reimburse' never lands as the mechanism, and the 60c-per-pound industry baseline it's being compared against never appears — which is the whole reason $2,000 sounds like a lot.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. On a call where the customer's stated worry is whether a stranger will handle an $800 television carefully, the email that shows him the mover's photo and name a few days out is the exact answer, and Jeline reached for a verbal reassurance instead ('our movers are not daily contracted workers. They are really well [trained] in this industry').
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

Clock start never explained. She gave the two-and-a-half-hour minimum and the fifteen-minute proration back to back and never said when the billable clock begins or ends — on a move between two San Antonio addresses where drive time is a live question.
No sense-check anywhere. The pricing block and the estimate ran back to back with no 'does that make sense?' — the customer's only input across both was 'Okay.'

No typical time range given to anchor the estimate. She went straight to 'I estimate your move to finish in three and a half to four and a half hours' without ever telling him what a two-bedroom normally takes, so he has no way to judge whether his job is easy, average, or hard — and no way to see that she was pricing it below a normal two-bedroom because there are no boxes.
Drive time never mentioned or factored. Two San Antonio addresses, 78258 to 78209, is a real cross-city haul and it never appeared in the estimate reasoning or as a trip-fee question.
Traffic never mentioned.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors to make four and a half hours feel concrete against the short furniture list he gave.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. And the opening was there: the customer said the move is furniture only, no boxes, which means he is doing all his own small-item transport already and would have been immediately receptive to 'anything small and loose — the drawers, the closet, the pictures off the walls — take a carload over yourself and it comes straight off your clock.' On a booked move, this speech is the single highest-value thing she could have said for the actual move-day outcome.
Hours and how to reach us never given. 'Just let us know through email' with no hours and no phone number.

The TV reassurance was left half-finished. She told him honestly that there is no case large enough — 'we do not have a TV case that can hold your 65 inch TV' — and then never told him what he could do about it. No suggestion to keep the original box if he has it, no offer to note it for the crew, no mention of whether he should transport it himself. The customer said this was his single biggest concern and the answer ended at 'we wrap them with layers of moving blankets.'
top_strength: Jeline runs the cleanest close in this week's sample and she is the only rep of eight to complete the email handoff properly. The booking attempt is textbook — availability, the no-risk framing, and a direct ask, in one breath: 'we can also put you now on our schedule for Saturday to secure your truck for next, for next week. Anyway, no deposit is required so no risk and securing your spot. So if something comes up, if ever you want to reschedule, just let us know you are free to do so. So with that, would you like to be on the schedule today?' No deposit isn't dropped as a fact here, it's used as the thing that makes yes costless — and she got the yes. Then she did what nobody else did: she named the arrival window and confirmed it ('our arrival window is between 8:30 AM to 9:00 AM. Are you okay with that schedule?'), collected both unit numbers, and set up the email as a verification step rather than a receipt — 'I'll be sending you now your confirmation email. So on that email there will be a bolted [bolded] list like the date and time that we agreed upon the addresses and your contact information. So if everything is good then we're good to go but that if you have any more questions or concern just let us know through email.' Bolded list, named contents, and an explicit ask for the customer to check it. That is the full rubric bullet, delivered once, cleanly, and it is the only time it appears across all eight calls. Her probe is also the second-strongest of the week and the best on physical access. She caught a contradiction in the form data and chased it instead of accepting it — the record said first floor, the customer said 'it's like on the first floor, but you have to go down the stairs. So it's kind of like the basement,' and rather than nodding she pinned the number: 'but there's only like one set of stairs.' Then she measured the walk in segments at both ends ('for the parking area, what's the distance to go to the stairs?' ... 'once we are on the like the basements... what's the distance to you get into your apartment?' ... 'can you tell me the distance from the parking to your apartment') and got real figures. She used the box anchor correctly ('normally for a two bedroom apartment we see 25 to 35 boxes. Do you think you would fall within that range?'), and when the customer surfaced his one real anxiety — a 65-inch, $800 television — she did not oversell. She told him the truth first ('we do not have a TV case that can hold your 65 inch TV'), explained the actual handling, and only then reached for the damage coverage. Leading with the limitation and following with the protection is the right order and it built trust: 'Okay, perfect.' She also used the customer's name three times across ten minutes, hit a warm close, and got an enthusiastic ending — 'Awesome, sounds good. Thank you so much.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Jeline closed the sale and left the differentiators on the table, and one of them was the direct answer to the only worry her customer expressed. He told her the thing he cares about is a 65-inch TV worth $800. She responded with damage coverage and a verbal 'our movers are not daily contracted workers.' The stronger answer was sitting right there: 'A few days before the move we'll email you a photo and a short bio of the actual movers coming to your place, so you'll know exactly who's handling that TV before they knock. And every move carries our No Worries Damage Coverage — up to two thousand dollars to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage. That's real coverage; most movers give you sixty cents a pound, which on a TV is about fifteen dollars.' That is three rubric bullets and a much better answer, in twenty seconds. Second priority: no Save Your Ass speech on a booked move, which is where it matters most. This one is booked, dated, and windowed — the move is happening, so every minute the customer shaves off the load is a minute off his actual bill, and his final line was effectively an offer to help ('Awesome, sounds good'). Furniture-only with no boxes means he has already decided to self-transport the small stuff; he just doesn't know what counts. 'Since you're handling your own boxes — anything loose and small, the stuff in the dresser drawers, the closet, pictures off the walls, take a carload or two over before we get there. Every one of those trips comes off the clock. Does that make sense?' That is ten points on the scorecard and real dollars off his invoice. Third, the pricing tiers. This is a Saturday at $206/hr and she never told him Sunday through Thursday is cheaper. He may have no flexibility, but he was never given the choice, and the rep two desks over offered exactly this to a customer who took it and saved money. State the rate per mover per hour, then the team number, then the tiers — every call. Fourth, the clock has a hole in it. Minimum and proration were both given; when the clock starts and stops was not. On a cross-city San Antonio move, 'the clock starts when we arrive at your door, not when we leave the shop' is the sentence that prevents a move-day argument. On estimate accuracy: no padding flag here, and the reasoning was sound — she cited the actual variables ('since we're coming from let's say a basement there will be like one side of stairs with a special items that we have to take extra care of going to a first floor apartment') and landed 3.5-4.5 hours. If anything this may run light: a two-bedroom is normally 3.5-5.5 hours and she quoted below that because there are no boxes, which is correct logic, but she never told the customer she was doing it. Say it out loud — 'a two-bedroom usually runs three and a half to five and a half, but with no boxes and short walks at both ends I'd put you at the low end, three and a half to four and a half' — because that sentence is what makes the customer trust the number and what makes a variance reviewable later. This one is worth pulling the actual on, since it booked.
phone_presence_notes: Warm, attentive and personally reassuring where it counted — she used the customer's name three times, answered the TV worry by addressing him directly ('65 inch just to inform you Logan...') and closed with 'I can assure you that we can take care of your TV,' which drew a genuine 'Okay, perfect' — though the delivery leans scripted in stretches and the pricing and estimate blocks ran without a single check-in.
